# You could have invented transformers from memory

Every layer is a memory store

[code] [interactive app]

Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.

How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?

In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.

The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity .

We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.

Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory .

## An outer product memory store #

The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,

where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$. 1

To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights. 2

Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer’s output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, so a step with learning rate $\eta$ is

This recurrence is a memory update: it updates the weights with a new memory with key $x$ and value $-\eta\bar y$. For more on this view, see Irie, Csordás & Schmidhuber , who express a linear layer trained by gradient descent as attention over all of its training inputs.

To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:

So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.

### Recall picks up interference #

So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?

Let’s assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then

meaning we get back the value of the target memory , the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.

If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.

What is the outer-product store’s capacity? Here’s an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference’s squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal’s, and

Setting this ratio to 1 gives a capacity of

once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.

Each bar below is one stored memory’s weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory’s weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we’ll build later in the post.

## How do we reduce interference? #

Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall. 3 To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to reduce interference .

The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store’s capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.

Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more selectively: every memory in a linear store contributes interference, even when its key has low similarity to the query, so we can improve recall by suppressing the less similar keys.

In the rest of the post, we’ll see that storing outer product memories more carefully gives us the optimal linear memory store, which has about twice the capacity. Recalling selectively via nonlinearities gives us MLPs and self-attention.

## The optimal linear memory store #

The outer-product store writes each memory without regard to the others. Instead, we can choose the weights $W$ so that recall fits all of the stored memories at once. This is a linear regression problem: 4

When we store more memories than the key dimension, $M > d_k$, the least-squares solution is

This is the outer-product store $V\transpose K$ with one change: before we compare the query with the keys, we multiply it by $(K\transpose K)\inverse$, which undoes the keys’ covariance $K\transpose K$. This whitens the keys, so the store no longer overweights directions that many keys share.

When $M \leq d_k$, the regression can fit every memory exactly, as long as the keys are linearly independent. So the optimal store recalls with no interference at all, even when the keys aren’t orthogonal.

When $M > d_k$, we start to get interference, since there are only $d_k$ directions for the memory store to work with. For random keys and values, our interference-to-signal ratio becomes

This ratio equals 1 at

so the optimal store’s capacity is twice as large as before!

When $M \leq d_k$. If the keys are linearly independent, the $M\times M$ matrix of inner products between keys, $KK\transpose$, is invertible, and

fits every memory exactly. When $M < d_k$, the problem is underconstrained and has infinitely many solutions, and this one is the min-norm solution. The rows $\tilde k_i\transpose$ of $(KK\transpose)\inverse K$ are known as the dual basis for the rows of $K$: by construction, $(KK\transpose)\inverse KK\transpose = I$, so $\tilde k_i\transpose k_j = \delta_{ij}$. Then $f(k_j) = \sum_i v_i\, \tilde k_i\transpose k_j = v_j$, so there is no interference and we have perfect recall.

When $M > d_k$. Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $W K\transpose K = V\transpose K$, so $W = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse$. Both solutions are $W = V\transpose (K\transpose)\pinv$, where $A\pinv$ denotes the pseudoinverse of $A$: $(K\transpose)\pinv = (KK\transpose)\inverse K$ when the keys are linearly independent, and $(K\transpose)\pinv = K(K\transpose K)\inverse$ when they span $\reals^{d_k}$.

Now we can analyze the interference of $f(k_j) = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$. For a stored key $k_j$, the weight on each value $v_i$ is $k_i\transpose (K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$, which is exactly entry $(i, j)$ of the $M\times M$ matrix $P = K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose$:

$P$ is the projection onto the column space of $K$, a $d_k$-dimensional subspace of $\reals^M$. Two facts about projections help us analyze the interference-to-signal ratio:

- The signal term: By the cyclic property of the trace, $$\sum_{j=1}^M P_{jj} = \trace{K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose} = \trace{(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose K} = \trace{I_{d_k}} = d_k,$$ so the $M$ signal weights add up to $d_k$. If the keys are random, no key is special, so $P_{jj} \approx d_k/M$.

- The interference term: $P$ is a symmetric projection matrix, so $P\transpose P = P^2 = P$. Then $$\sum_{i\neq j} P_{ij}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^M P_{ij}^2 - P_{jj}^2 = (P\transpose P)_{jj} - P_{jj}^2 = P_{jj} - P_{jj}^2 \approx \frac{d_k}{M} - \parens*{\frac{d_k}{M}}^2.$$

If the values are random with similar lengths,

Compared to the outer-product store’s $\sqrt{M/d_k}$, the $-1$ is the $d_k$ memories’ worth of interference that the optimal store cancels.

We can check our predictions numerically. We randomly sample $M$ memories with unit-length keys in $d_k = 64$ dimensions, query the memory store with one of the stored keys, and measure the interference-to-signal ratio:

The outer-product store reaches its capacity at $M \approx d_k = 64$. The optimal store recalls exactly up to $M = d_k$. Past that, its interference rises from zero like $\sqrt{M/d_k - 1}$, and the store reaches its capacity near $M = 2d_k = 128$, as predicted. Since it cancels a fixed number of memories’ worth of interference, the gap between the two stores shrinks as $M$ grows.

This optimal memory store is still linear in the similarities though. It must scale small and large similarities by the same factor. To do better, we need to change how the store recalls.

## MLP as a nonlinear memory store #

A linear memory store recalls

If we had a way to suppress the weight when $k_i\transpose x$ is small, then we can reduce the amount of interference from low similarity keys.

Let’s pass each similarity through a nonlinear function $\sigma$ before computing the weighted sum of values:

We just rediscovered a two-layer MLP from first principles! The rows of the first weight matrix are the keys, the columns of the second weight matrix are the values. Sukhbaatar et al. pointed out this resemblance between feedforward layers and memory stores, and Geva et al. found that the feedforward layers in trained transformers often work this way, with keys firing on recognizable patterns in the input.

Ideally, the gating function $\sigma$ is chosen such that when the similarity is low ($k_i\transpose x \sim 0$ or even when $k_i\transpose x < 0$), its corresponding term in the sum gets suppressed to reduce interference. A ReLU activation zeros out keys with negative similarities, and adding a bias allows shifting that threshold 5 . A squared ReLU activation further suppresses the keys with similarities close to zero. A similarity of 0.1 becomes 0.01, while a similarity of 1 stays 1. In fact, squared ReLUs are one of the lesser known but established-at-scale improvements to MLP activations ( So et al. ).

A squared ReLU MLP is a GLU MLP whose gate and input projection share weights, since $\operatorname{ReLU}(Kx)^2 = \operatorname{ReLU}(Kx) \odot Kx$. The SwiGLU MLPs in today’s language models give the gate its own weights and use a Swish activation in place of the ReLU.

# Matrix gradients, without the pain

A simple trick for deriving gradients without drowning in subscripts

In this post I want to share a simple trick to make computing gradients and backward passes mechanical, without drowning in indices and ruining your eyesight.

To start with, let’s remember how we all first learned to compute gradients. Suppose we have a linear layer $Y = XW$, where $X$ is an $N\times D$ batch of inputs and $W$ is a $D\times F$ weight matrix, followed by some scalar loss $L(Y) \in \reals$. Suppose you already know the gradient of the loss with respect to the outputs, $\grad L(Y)$, an $N\times F$ matrix.

Write $\Lcal(W) = L(XW)$ for the loss as a function of the weights, with $X$ held fixed. Throughout the post, $L$ takes a layer’s output, and $\Lcal$ is the loss as a function of whatever we’re differentiating.

What’s the gradient of the loss with respect to $W$, $\grad \Lcal(W)$?

The rote way is to compute the answer one entry at a time.

Pick an entry $W_{ab}$ and apply the chain rule over every entry of $Y$, where $\partial L/\partial Y_{ij}$ is entry $(i,j)$ of $\grad L(Y)$:

Next, expand $Y_{ij} = \sum_k X_{ik}W_{kj}$ to find that $\partial Y_{ij}/\partial W_{ab}$ is $X_{ia}$ when $j = b$ and zero otherwise. That collapses the sum to

The last step is to recognize this sum as a matrix product. The index $i$ is summed over, but it sits first on both $X$ and $\grad L(Y)$, so one of them must be transposed. After staring at it, you land on $\grad \Lcal(W) = X\transpose \grad L(Y)$. That’s a lot of work for one of the simplest layers there is .

Here’s how I would compute the gradient (I’ll explain the notation later):

So $\grad \Lcal(W) = X\transpose \grad L(Y)$. There are no indices, and the transpose comes from moving $X$ across the inner product. Magical , right?

By the end of the post, you will understand the machinery behind this trick. The trick rests on clearly understanding two related ideas:

- the derivative at a point, which is a linear function .

- the gradient at a point, which is the vector that, when paired with an inner product, represents the derivative.

With these two ideas, we can compute gradient by following the same recipe .

## The derivative at a point is a linear function #

Let $f: \reals^D \to \reals^{D'}$ be a function with vector input and vector output. The derivative of $f$ at some point $x\in \reals^D$ is a linear function written $\dd f_x: \reals^D \to \reals^{D'}$. It is the best linear approximation of how $f$ changes near $x$.

What does it mean to be the best linear approximation? Suppose you know $f(x)$ and you want to estimate $f(x + \dd x)$ for some small change $\dd x \in \reals^D$. Here $\dd x$ is a regular ol’ vector like any other. We could have written $\Delta x$, but the “differential” notation will pay off later. Given the small change $\dd x$, $\dd f_x$ outputs the first-order change in $f$:

where the residual $r(\dd x)$ decays faster than $\dd x$. For small changes $\dd x$, the change in the output is approximately the linear function $\dd f_x$ applied to $\dd x$: $f(x+\dd x) - f(x) \approx \dd_x f(\dd x)$.

Recall that every linear function between $\reals^D$ and $\reals^{D'}$ can be written as a matrix. For the derivative at a point $x$, $\dd f_x$, its matrix representation is the Jacobian $J_f(x)$:

Its entries are $(J_f(x))_{ij} = (\dd f_x(e_j))_i$, where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector. Sometimes this is written as $J_f(x)_{ij} = \partial_j f_i(x)$. In automatic differentiation, multiplying the Jacobian by a vector like this is called a Jacobian-vector product, or forward-mode differentiation.

### Derivatives follow the chain rule #

Suppose $f = g\circ h$, where $g$ and $h$ are vector-valued functions with vector-valued inputs and outputs. Define $y = h(x)$. Then the chain rule says:

In words: push the small change $\dd x$ through $h$’s derivative to get the change in $h$, then push the change in $h$ through $g$’s derivative to get the overall change in $f$.

To talk about gradients, we first need inner products.

## Inner products turn vectors into numbers #

The inner product of two vectors $a, b \in \reals^D$ is $\inner{a}{b} = a\transpose b = \sum_i a_i b_i$. For two matrices of the same shape, the standard inner product does the same thing, multiplying matching entries and summing them:

- A matrix can hop to the other side of an inner product by transposing: $\inner{a}{Mb} = \inner{M\transpose a}{b}$ for vectors, and $\inner{A}{MB} = \inner{M\transpose A}{B}$ for matrices.

- A scalar equals its own transpose, and its own trace: any scalar $c$ can be rewritten as $\trace{c}$.

- The trace is unchanged when you cycle a product: $\trace{ABC} = \trace{CAB} = \trace{BCA}$. Only cycling works; in general $\trace{ABC} \neq \trace{ACB}$.

- Inner products are linear in each argument, so constants and sums pull out.

These properties will help us “move terms around” when computing gradients via inner products.

## The gradient represents the derivative #

The gradient is only defined for scalar-valued functions , such as the loss function $L$ we saw at the beginning. So let’s consider a function $f: \reals^D\to \reals$. The derivative of $f$ at $x$, $\dd f_x$, is a linear function from $\reals^D$ to $\reals$.

Definition: the gradient

The gradient of $f$ at $x$, written $\grad f(x)$, is the unique vector in $\reals^D$ such that for every $\dd x\in \reals^D$:

In other words, the inner product of $\dd x$ with the gradient vector gives the approximate change in $f$.

Why does such a vector exist, and why is it unique? Plug in the basis vector $\dd x = e_i$. The $i$th entry of $\grad f(x)$ must equal $\dd f_x(e_i)$, which is the partial derivative $\partial f/\partial x_i$. So the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives you already know, and this definition just describes it without indices. For a matrix input $W$, the same argument says entry $(i,j)$ of $\grad f(W)$ is $\partial f/\partial W_{ij}$. In every case, the gradient vector always has the same shape as the variable it’s taken with respect to .

For a fixed $x$, $\dd f_x$ takes an input $\dd x$ and returns a number. This is why a derivative acts like the row vector $\grad f(x)\transpose$, while $\grad f(x)$ itself is a column vector .

## How to compute gradients without indices #

Characterizing the gradient as a dual representation of the derivative gives us a simple way to compute gradients by first computing derivatives (which lets us use the chain rule):

- Compute the derivative at a point $\dd f_x(\dd x)$. 1

- Rearrange the result into the form $\inner{\textit{something}}{\dd x}$, and read off the $\textit{something}$. Uniqueness guarantees that the $\textit{something}$ is the gradient.

### Example: the gradient of a quadratic form #

Let $f(x) = x\transpose A x$, where $A$ is a $D\times D$ matrix. We want $\grad f(x)$.

Before we start, let’s define our differential notation/shorthand, which we’ll use in our derivations.

Let $g(x) = Ax$. Its derivative applied to a small change $\dd x$ is $\dd g_x(\dd x) = A\,\dd x$, because $g$ is linear, so its best linear approximation is itself. Differential notation writes this as $\dd(Ax) = A\,\dd x$, which says “the derivative of the anonymous function $x \mapsto Ax$, applied to $\dd x$, is $A$ times $\dd x$.” In general, $\dd(\text{expression})$ means the derivative of $x \mapsto \text{expression}$ applied to $\dd x$ 2 .

Let’s now return to our $f(x) = x\transpose A x$. Using the product rule and differential notation, step 1 is one line:

For step 2, we rewrite the result as an inner product with $\dd x$. The first term is a scalar, so it equals its own transpose, $(\dd x)\transpose Ax = x\transpose A\transpose \dd x$. So

By uniqueness of the gradient, $\grad f(x) = (A +A\transpose)x$.

## Backprop the simple way using the chain rule #

I remember being confused why the chain rule we learned for derivatives didn’t work exactly for gradients. Gradients seemed to obey something that only resembled the chain rule. For example, in single-variable calculus the chain rule says $(g\circ h)'(x) = g'(h(x))\, h'(x)$: the outer derivative times the inner derivative. Now take $\Lcal(x) = L(Wx)$ for a scalar loss $L$ and a matrix $W$. Its gradient is

The inner derivative $W$ shows up transposed, and it comes before the outer gradient instead of after. Where did the transpose come from, and why did the order flip? People often just wave it off as “oh it has to be like this to make the shapes work out.

We can do better.

Turns out, derivatives compose by the chain rule, but gradients compose via vector-Jacobian products. Suppose $f = g\circ h$ is scalar-valued, so $g$ is scalar-valued but $h$ need not be. For any $x\in \reals^D$ and any small change $\dd x\in \reals^D$, define $y=h(x)$ and $\dd y = \dd h_x(\dd x)$. The chain rule reads $\dd f_x(\dd x) = \dd g_y(\dd y)$. Writing both sides with the definition of the gradient gives:

for every small change $\dd x$, where $\dd y = \dd h_x(\dd x)$. This is the chain rule in inner-product form.

We can solve this equation for $\grad f(x)$, given $\grad g(y)$, just like backprop. To do this, express $\dd y$ in terms of $\dd x$ on the right-hand side, then rearrange until it reads $\inner{\textit{something}}{\dd x}$. That something is $\grad f(x)$.

Let’s see how to do this in general. First write the derivative of $h$ as its Jacobian, $\dd y = J_h(x)\,\dd x$ (see the Jacobian aside above), and hop it across the inner product:

By uniqueness of the gradient, we arrive at the chain rule for gradients:

The chain rule for gradient

This rule is the basis of backprop. 3 Each layer takes the gradient flowing back from the layer above, $\grad g(y)$, and multiplies it by its own transposed Jacobian to get the gradient to pass further back. In practice you avoid materializing $J_h$, which could be enormous.

Writing $\grad$ everywhere gets heavy, so from here on I’ll use bars: $\bar y := \grad L(y)$ is the gradient of the loss with respect to an intermediate value $y$, and likewise $\bar x := \grad \Lcal(x)$ and $\bar W := \grad \Lcal(W)$ for whatever we’re differentiating. This bar notation comes from reverse-mode automatic differentiation, where $\bar y$ is called the adjoint of $y$ 4 .

### Example: the gradient with respect to a vector #

Take a single input instead of a batch: the layer is $y = Wx$, where $x$ is a column vector (e.g. a data point) and $W$ is a fixed $F\times D$ weight matrix, and $L(y)$ is a scalar loss on the output. Write $\Lcal(x) = L(Wx)$ for the loss as a function of the input. We want $\bar x$, and we know $\bar y$. Since $y = Wx$, $\dd y = W\dd x$. Then

By uniqueness of the gradient, the gradient of the loss with respect to the input is $\bar x = W\transpose \bar y$.

In the example above, $\dd \Lcal_x(\dd x) = \bar y\transpose W\, \dd x$, and $W$ is the Jacobian of the inner function $x\mapsto Wx$. There are two orders in which to compute this product:

- A Jacobian-vector product computes $W\dd x$ first, then takes the inner product with $\bar y$. This is forward-mode differentiation, and it handles one direction $\dd x$ at a time.

- A vector-Jacobian product computes $\bar y\transpose W$ first. This result does not depend on $\dd x$ at all, and its transpose is the full gradient $W\transpose\bar y$. This is reverse-mode differentiation, also called backpropagation.

One vector-Jacobian product gives the whole gradient, while forward mode would need one Jacobian-vector product per input dimension. That is why neural networks are trained with backpropagation.

# Put a price on research breakthroughs

How frontier labs, neolabs, and investors can all win

Neolabs today are being asked to pull off two moonshots at once. Their investors want both a research breakthrough and a venture-scale business, even though each of those alone is a 1 in 100 outcome. Asking for both makes their chances 1 in 10,000.

I think there’s a better alternative, one that borrows from the way pharma handles risky R&D and lets frontier labs, neolabs, and investors all come out ahead.

## Frontier labs want to scale up what works #

Today, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind are caught in a neck-and-neck race on model quality and intelligence. Every release needs to exceed expectations, or at least meet what competitors are doing. So they’d rather spend their resources scaling things that are proven to work , like improving data pipelines, building infrastructure for larger runs, and buying ever-more compute. However, researchers often want to work on “the next big thing”, new paradigms that could lead to a discontinuous jump in intelligence. As a result, there’s often tension between what the market needs them to ship and what researchers want to focus on.

## Neolabs are asked to do two things at once #

In the past year, many senior researchers who want to pursue these bets have started neolabs , nascent AI startups focused on big research bets, usually funded with a lot of money before they have a product or revenue, so they can pay for compute and salaries. That way they can chase the big idea with venture-scale resources.

On the surface, investors are betting that a neolab becomes the next OpenAI or Anthropic. They remind themselves that Anthropic was once a neolab too, started by a group of researchers who left OpenAI and raised hundreds of millions of dollars before they had a product. Privately though, most of them will admit the odds of a repeat are next to none, even with world-class researchers and engineers.

Running a research team is a different job from scaling a company. Researchers usually aren’t great at product, go-to-market, operations, logistics, etc., all the things that traditionally matter for a sustainable company. ( Ali Ghodsi at Databricks is a good exception.)

However, neolabs are expected to do both: make a breakthrough and scale a product. Sometimes this splits a company in two, with half the people wanting to build and sell and the other half wanting to do research and build ASI. Focus and alignment are the biggest advantages a startup has over better-funded incumbents, but this expectation can take a toll on both.

Investors who expect their neolab to do both will likely be disappointed when it does neither.

One radical move is to admit that a neolab is just going to do world-class, groundbreaking research. Expect close to zero revenue and let them cook. If they succeed, they get acquired or acquihired .

The catch is that this doesn’t work for investors. A VC needs companies that can return the entire fund, and it’s hard to promise LPs that an acquihire will do that, especially at the sky-high multibillion valuations neolabs raise at today.

## Pharma already solved a version of this #

Drug development has dealt with a similar problem for decades. Companies regularly risk hundreds of millions of dollars in R&D on a drug that might pay off billions. A drug can pass early trials and still fail before FDA approval, usually because it doesn’t work well enough, and sometimes because of side effects or manufacturing problems.

Pharma handles this by splitting the work. Smaller biotech companies take on the risk of discovery and development. If a drug works, a big pharma company acquires the startup or buys the drug as IP. The big company doubles down on what it’s good at, which is producing and distributing drugs at scale. The small company gets to do the science without having to invent a business model. A small biotech’s business model comes down to one question: can we make this drug work or not?

The division of labor works. Of the drugs the FDA approved from 2013 to 2022, small companies with under \$500M in revenue originated 52% , while the biggest companies, with over \$10B in revenue, originated 36% 1 .

Biotech investors have made money this way for decades. Many of their biggest wins come from getting acquired, not from growing into the next Pfizer.

## Pre-registered acquisitions #

What’s missing today is a promise. The people who start, join, or fund a neolab need to know, before they take the risk, that a big payoff is waiting if the research works.

Frontier labs could make that promise ahead of time through pre-registered acquisitions . This kind of promise is also called “ pull funding ”. Push funding pays for research up front, like a grant or a VC round. Pull funding promises to pay for the result once it exists. In 1714, the British government promised £20,000 to anyone who could find a ship’s longitude at sea, and a self-taught clockmaker named John Harrison responded by inventing a clock that kept accurate time on a rolling ship. In 2009, five countries and the Gates Foundation promised \$1.5B to any company that could supply poor countries with pneumococcal vaccines at \$3.50 a dose or less, and vaccine makers responded with enough supply to immunize more than 150 million children.

Big companies have always bought startups for their patents or their people. What’s different about AI research is the cost of finding out whether an idea works. A software founder can test an idea on a laptop. Testing a new training method at a scale that matters takes a training run that can cost tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, and the cost of the largest runs has grown 2.4x a year since 2016 . Nobody spends that much on a guess without knowing what success is worth. The stakes are also bigger than any one company’s exit. A breakthrough in how models learn ends up in systems that hundreds of millions of people use every day, so how we pay for that research decides how fast it happens and who gets to do it.

I can see this playing out in two ways:

- Open offers. A frontier lab publishes a target anyone can check and commits to acquiring the first team that hits it, at a set price. OpenAI’s Parameter Golf challenge is a small version of this, with job interviews for standout entrants instead of an acquisition.

- Private options. A frontier lab and one neolab agree on a scoped goal up front. The lab gets the right to buy the neolab at a set price if the goal is met, and pays a fallback fee if it walks away. SpaceX’s option to buy Cursor had this structure: \$60B if SpaceX bought, or \$10B for the work if it didn’t. SpaceX bought it .

In both cases, the target can be a new capability, like a benchmark score, or something the lab can’t easily build itself, like a dataset, a set of RL environments , or a regulatory approval.

Here’s what an open offer could look like. Say a frontier lab posts: “We’ll acquire any team that matches our last-generation model on this eval suite using a tenth of the training compute, for \$2B. Train from scratch, no distilling from anyone’s frontier model, and the offer is good through 2027.” The price makes sense, because the largest training runs are on track to cost more than \$1B each by 2027 , so cutting the compute for every future run by 10x is worth far more than \$2B.

## Why would a frontier lab commit? #

The obvious question is why a lab would name a price before seeing results, when it could wait and buy whatever works.

After a breakthrough, it’s too late. Training recipes can’t be patented, so once a team shows a lab how it did something, the lab doesn’t need the team anymore. No sensible team will show its work without a price agreed first, and no lab will pay for something it hasn’t seen. This is called Arrow’s information paradox . Naming the price in advance breaks the deadlock: the team knows what it gets, and the lab gets to check the result before it pays.

## A win-win-win solution #

Pre-registered acquisitions let everyone come out ahead.

The frontier labs get to:

- Keep scaling what works.

- Bet on 0-to-1 breakthroughs without funding every long shot themselves.

Neolabs and their researchers get to:

- Chase unproven but high-potential bets that could lead to a breakthrough, with funding behind them.

- Skip product-market fit and go-to-market, and spend their time on the research they’re best at and most excited about.

- Stay internally aligned, because everyone knows they can win just by making a breakthrough.

- Form a team, or go solo, and take a shot at a published target. Smaller targets work too: if a lab posts \$100M for a new set of RL environments, spending \$100k on compute to try is a reasonable bet.

Investors get to:

- Take on less market risk, because if their team gets there first, there’s a committed buyer at a known price.

- Value a neolab against the acquisition price. That won’t justify a \$5B seed round, but it will justify a \$100M one, and a \$2B exit on a \$100M entry returns the fund.

An open offer is also a floor, not a ceiling. If a team hits the target and would rather build a business around what it made, it can turn the offer down.

## Making the implicit explicit #

Some version of this already exists. Every past acquisition and acquihire , like Google’s \$2.4B Windsurf deal , sets an implicit anchor for what a research team can exit for, and neolabs point to those anchors to justify their valuations. A pre-registered acquisition just makes that explicit, reducing the uncertainty for everyone.

Right now a neolab has to win at research and at business, two moonshots at once. Put a price on the breakthrough and it only has to win one. The payoff is smaller than becoming the next Anthropic, but the odds go from 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100, and that’s a bet you can build a team around.

So, frontier labs: what would you pay for a training run that costs a tenth as much? Name a price.

- One caveat: A drug is easy to patent, and an AI training recipe mostly isn’t . So in AI the payoff can’t just be a sale of IP. It has to be an acquisition, either of the team itself or of a moat that’s hard to copy, like regulatory approvals, unique data, or unique physical infrastructure. ↩︎

# The model is the company

Why the first autonomous companies will be startups

Picture two founders starting a company today.

One scales by hiring. Each person sees a small part of the company and develops expertise that stays in their head. Everyone has a different perspective on what’s the right thing to do and it takes a while for them to reach a consensus. Over time, the company gets bigger. No single person holds the full picture and coordination overhead builds up.

The other founder does something different. They build an AI-native company. They structure every decision and action as the output of a superintelligent model and log every outcome. Although the setup took more effort, the model has complete context of the business and learns to run it over time.

After three years, the first company has a hundred people who each hold a piece of the puzzle. Their shared understanding is scattered across Slack threads, undocumented meetings, and the minds of employees who might leave tomorrow. The second company, however, is a unified operating system that has compounded every outcome from every decision for a thousand days. Always getting smarter. Always getting faster. Always getting better.

One of these companies ends up eating the other.

## Companies are information processors #

A company is just a group of actors working together as one legal entity. The inhabitants transform data into reports, coordinate work, and decide what action to take. Remove the internal relationships and it just comes down to information processing. Signals come in, decisions are made, and actions go out.

Much of the work in running a company is informational, whether it’s engineering, product, strategy, operations, finance, marketing, sales, legal, hiring, or logistics. But processing information is exactly what models are best at.

The inevitable conclusion as AI capability improves exponentially is that one day the model doesn’t just assist with these functions but becomes the company itself. A model that is both the orchestrator and the actor.

When that day comes, the company becomes the harness and the model becomes the company .

## The last mile #

The world is already moving in this direction. Foundation models can work for hours and soon days . Agents are managing logistics for supply chains and running vending machine businesses . Researchers are making steady progress on continual learning . So why don’t we have this today?

There are three barriers: one scientific, one engineering, and one sociological.

The scientific barrier is that models don’t yet learn from their experience the way we do. Until recently, most models learned by imitating humans (see imitation learning ). But you can’t learn to run a company by watching others do it. You need to learn from your own mistakes. Recent advances in reinforcement learning are closing this gap, and have produced a new generation of agents. AI can finally take actions reliably. But unlike us, AI still separates learning from acting. Researchers must train the model in a simulated environment before deploying it into production. The model is frozen, and its core capabilities and knowledge cannot adapt to what it sees. As a result, an AI agent today is as capable on day one thousand as it was on day one. To solve this problem, we need new research to unlock continual learning.

The engineering barrier is building a harness that captures every action and outcome of a company as training signal. A company is a complex distributed system. Dozens of processes run in parallel. Imagine logging every customer interaction, every operational decision, and every sale as a live feedback loop that shapes the model’s behavior in real time. We don’t have this infrastructure yet, but it’s a solvable engineering problem. In fact, this kind of harness is being built as we speak (see OpenAI Frontier ).

The last barrier, the sociological one, is different. It may not be solvable at all, at least by incumbent companies.

## No one will build this willingly #

Let me tell you a secret. Companies are not actually optimized for shareholder value. They are optimized for the people working there. Careers are built on judgement, taste, and the accumulation of decision-making power.

Now imagine telling these people that the optimal future for their company is one that doesn’t include them.

No one will build this willingly. Managers may try their best to automate the work beneath them, but they will resist replacing themselves. The incentives are perfectly misaligned, a classic principal-agent problem. In fact, we’ve seen this before in finance. Portfolio managers are careful to keep their decision-making processes to themselves. Quants are rumored to keep their code undocumented on purpose. Making your expertise legible in the age of learning machines is simply self-obsolescence. Incumbents will try, but they will hit a ceiling set by the people who have the most to lose. No one will willingly fire themselves, no matter how sincere they may sound .

## Starting from scratch #

The science is close. The engineering is solvable. The only barrier left is a deeply human one.

The first autonomous companies won’t be built by the incumbents who have the most to gain. They’ll be built by hyperscaling startups with no one to replace.
